thread.title: Facebook Stock Is Up Because Earnings Crushed Expectations

title: Facebook Stock Is Up Because Earnings Crushed Expectations
text:
Facebook Stock Is Up Because Earnings Crushed Expectations By Updated Jan. 30, 2019 5:30 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Loic Venance/AFP/Getty Images Text size
Facebook stock (ticker: FB) surged in after-hours trading after the social networking giant reported better-than-expected fiscal fourth-quarter earnings.
The back story. Facebook has endured two years of eviscerating headlines over privacy and data snafus that pulverized its stock 22% over the past year, and called into question the management team of Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg and Chief Operating Officer Sheryl Sandberg. And yet, the company’s stock has rebounded 15% in 2019 as a testament to its dominance in social media and No. 2 status in online advertising, behind only Alphabet’s (GOOGL) Google.
The numbers. Late Wednesday, Facebook reported a fiscal fourth-quarter profit of $2.38 a share, beating Wall Street’s forecast for $2.18. Revenue of $16.91 billion also topped expectations for $16.39 billion. Advertising revenue, the lifeblood of Facebook’s business, improved 30% to $16.6 billion. Monthly active users, a key barometer for advertising sales, grew 9% to 2.32 billion—above analysts’ estimates of 2.31 billion. Newsletter Sign-up
“Our community and business continue to grow. We’ve fundamentally changed how we run our company to focus on the biggest social issues, and we’re investing more to build new and inspiring ways for people to connect,” Zuckerberg said in a statement.
Historical data. Facebook has exceeded analysts’ earnings-per-share estimates 96% of the time since it went public in 2012, and it has beaten sales estimates 88% of the time. But it missed on sales the two quarters prior to Thursday’s report, leading to a 31% drop in its stock price since July 25.
Looking ahead. Facebook shares were up 11% in after-hours trading.
In a conference call following the earnings release, Zuckerberg predicted greater mainstream use of Watch, its video-on-demand service; new opportunities in shopping revenue via Instagram; and developments in augmented and virtual reality to enhance the Facebook experience.
What’s on the horizon. Zuckerberg is asserting his control over the company, with the approval of many employees, despite a series of scandals the past two years. On Wednesday, Apple (AAPL) revoked some of Facebook’s developer privileges because of a data-collecting app. Facebook denied any wrongdoing in an emailed statement to Barron’s .
Late last week, The New York Times reported Zuckerberg plans to integrate Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger, stitching together their technical infrastructure while continuing to operate the services as stand-alone apps. The move is intended to strengthen Facebook’s grip on more than 2.6 billion users by early 2020. But it could raise “alarm bells” over privacy issues, says Ray Walsh, digital privacy officer at cybersecurity firm BestVPN.com.
“While many consumers may abstain from Facebook for privacy reasons, huge numbers of those people are happy to use WhatsApp for its secure end-to-end encrypted messaging,” Walsh said in an email to Barron’s . “What is interesting, is that in order to join WhatsApp users must hand over their name and phone number to the company that owns WhatsApp—Facebook.”
Indeed, Zuckerberg again defended Facebook’s model of targeted ads for its active users, in an op-ed in The Wall Street Journal last week.
Some polls, meanwhile, underscore that venture-capitalist and early Facebook investor Roger McNamee and other critical former Facebook executives may represent a vocal minority. Only 17% of 985 Facebook employees believe scandals involving Zuckerberg have devalued Facebook, and 83% of 735 the company’s employees think he should remain CEO, according to Blind, an anonymous social networking app that conducted the two polls Jan. 10 to 18. By comparison, more than half (56%) of 11,795 tech employees polled believe Zuckerberg devalued Facebook, and 53% of 8,229 people think he should remain CEO.
